steps.title: If money was sent, call your bank's fraud line now
steps.detail: Call the fraud line on the back of your bank card or on your contacts card. Say you sent a payment because of a fake email and ask them to recall or stop the transfer.
steps.why: Banks can sometimes stop or recall a transfer, but only in the first hours. The sooner they know, the better the chance.
steps.do_not: Do not wait until you are sure. Call first, then check the details.

steps.title: Do not reply to the email
steps.detail: Leave the email as it is. Do not answer it, click its links or open its attachments.
steps.why: The person who wrote it may control that address. A reply tells them you noticed and gives them more time.
steps.do_not: Do not call phone numbers or use contact details from the suspicious email.

steps.title: Check with the real person using a number you already have
steps.detail: Call the supplier, client or manager on a number from an old invoice, their website or your contacts card. Ask if they really sent the request.
steps.why: Fake emails often copy a real name and logo. A call on a number you trust is the quickest way to know.

steps.title: Keep the email and the payment details
steps.detail: Do not delete anything. Write down the amount, date, time and the bank account the money went to. Take a photo of the email on screen.
steps.why: Your bank, the police and your insurer will ask for these exact details.
steps.do_not: Do not delete the email or empty your trash.

steps.title: Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov
steps.detail: From a clean device, file a complaint at ic3.gov. Include the amount, the date and the bank account details of the transfer.
steps.why: The FBI works with banks to try to freeze stolen money. Quick reports help.

steps.title: Change your email password and turn on two-step login
steps.detail: From a clean device, change the password of the email account involved. Turn on two-step login (a code on your phone).
steps.why: Attackers often get into a real mailbox first, then send fake invoices from it.

steps.title: Ask your IT contact to check the mailbox
steps.detail: Ask them to look for forwarding rules, unknown sign-ins and messages you did not send.
steps.why: Attackers often add hidden rules that forward or delete replies, so you do not see warnings.

steps.title: Call your IT contact
steps.detail: Tell them what happened and when. Read them your notes. Follow their advice on what to check next.
steps.why: They can check whether other accounts or computers are affected.

steps.title: Warn everyone who pays bills
steps.detail: Tell the people who pay invoices what happened. From now on, any change of bank details is confirmed by phone on a known number.
steps.why: The same attackers often try again with a new email.

steps.title: Call your insurance company
steps.detail: If you have cyber or business insurance, call their claims line and say you may have lost money to email fraud.
steps.why: Many policies need quick notice, and some cover this kind of loss.

steps.title: Report it to the FTC
steps.detail: From a clean device, report the scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
steps.why: Reports help the FTC warn other businesses about the same scam.

steps.title: Outside the US? Report it in your country
steps.detail: In Canada, report it to the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security at cyber.gc.ca and to your local police. In France, get help at cybermalveillance.gouv.fr.
steps.why: National services can help you report the crime and recover.
